front: What is the core question Anderson's abstract poses?
back: Given hardware support for atomic instructions, are there efficient software spin-waiting algorithms, or is more complex hardware support needed for performance?

front: What analogy frames Anderson's method in the abstract?
back: Arbitration for control of a lock is in many ways similar to arbitration for control of a network connecting a distributed system, so the paper applies static and dynamic network-arbitration methods to spin locks.

front: What three contributions does Anderson's abstract preview?
back: The CSMA-derived delay methods; a novel software queueing method (a unique sequence number per arriving processor); and several hardware solutions that reduce the cost of spin-waiting.

front: Which commercially successful shared-memory multiprocessors does Anderson name in the introduction?
back: The Sequent Symmetry, Alliant FX, and BBN Butterfly.

front: Which research-vehicle multiprocessors does Anderson name in the introduction?
back: The DEC SRC Firefly, Illinois Cedar, IBM RP3, and Wisconsin Multicube.

front: Why do virtually all shared-memory multiprocessors provide hardware atomic instructions, per Anderson?
back: Because pure software mutual exclusion is expensive (he cites Lamport's fast mutual exclusion algorithm).

front: What two distinct purposes do atomic instructions serve, per Anderson (and which does the lecture use)?
back: (1) If the operation on shared data is simple enough, it is encapsulated in a single atomic instruction so mutual exclusion is guaranteed directly in hardware; (2) for critical sections longer than one instruction, atomics arbitrate acquiring a lock while waiting is done in software. The notes use only the second.

front: In exactly which two situations is spin-waiting (vs blocking) the right choice, per Anderson?
back: When the critical section is small (so the expected wait is less than the cost of blocking and resuming), or when there is no other work for the processor to do.

front: What thesis (that contention performance does not matter) does Anderson state before rebutting it?
back: That a highly parallel application by definition has no heavily contended lock, and a bottleneck lock should be removed by redesigning the algorithm rather than by adding processors.

text:
Anderson's four situations where spin-lock contention performance does matter:
  1. {{c1::A heavily utilized lock prevents peak performance, because the average number of spinners grows as the lock approaches saturation}}
  2. {{c2::Bursty arrivals cause temporarily long queues and bad short-term performance, even without a long-term bottleneck}}
  3. {{c3::An OS cannot control the rate of system calls, so normally quiet locks become contended at high load}}
  4. {{c4::On a multiprogrammed multiprocessor, a naive user can ruin everyone's performance by combining a bottleneck critical section, many processors, and an inefficient spin lock}}
Anderson states the spin-lock tradeoff: the more frequently a processor tries to acquire a lock, the {{c1::faster it will be acquired}}, but the {{c2::more other processors will be disrupted}}.

Anderson's six architecture types:
  1. Multistage interconnection network {{c1::without coherent caches}}
  2. Multistage network {{c2::with invalidation-based coherence using remote directories}}
  3. Bus {{c3::without coherent caches}}
  4. Bus with {{c4::snoopy write-through invalidation}}
  5. Bus with {{c5::snoopy write-back invalidation}}
  6. Bus with {{c6::snoopy distributed-write coherence}}
extra: The notes compress these into interconnect vs bus and write-update vs write-invalidate.
source: Section II: Range of multiprocessor architectures considered

front: What simplifying assumption does Anderson state once and use throughout Section II?
back: Processors block when making a read request to memory.
source: Section II: Range of multiprocessor architectures considered

front: What is Anderson's term for what the notes call write-update?
back: Distributed-write (also write-broadcast); the notes use write-update.
source: Section II: Range of multiprocessor architectures considered

front: Into what four services does Anderson decompose an atomic read-modify-write?
back: The read, the write, arbitration between simultaneous requests, and some state that blocks further accesses while the instruction executes. Most multiprocessors collapse these into one or two bus or network transactions.
source: II.A: Common hardware support for mutual exclusion

front: On a multistage network, how can the delay of an atomic be cut, and which machines do this?
back: The computation can be done remotely by an ALU attached to each memory module ("fetch and op"); the Butterfly and RP3 implement this.
source: II.A: Common hardware support for mutual exclusion

front: On a single bus, what mechanism lets an atomic block other atomics without holding the whole bus?
back: A processor acquires the bus and raises an "atomic bus line" before the atomic; the line is held while the value is computed to block other atomics, but the bus is released so normal memory requests proceed, and waiting atomics only re-arbitrate when the line drops.
source: II.A: Common hardware support for mutual exclusion

front: Why does the Firefly have a separate arbitration mechanism for its atomic bus line under distributed-write?
back: With distributed-write the block an atomic needs is usually already cached, so the initial read is usually unnecessary; piggy-backing the atomic-bus-line arbitration on top of bus arbitration would then waste bus cycles.
source: II.A: Common hardware support for mutual exclusion

front: With invalidation-based coherence, what can acquiring the atomic bus line be overlapped with, and when does the invalidation happen?
back: It can be overlapped with the signal to invalidate other cache copies (even if the lock value is cached). The invalidation happens before the instruction executes, so it occurs even if the instruction does not change the value.
source: II.A: Common hardware support for mutual exclusion

front: Per Anderson, is a correct simple spin lock hard to write, and where is the difficulty?
back: No; a correct simple spin lock is relatively straightforward (test-and-set to acquire, atomic clear to release). The difficulty is efficiency, not correctness.
source: Section III: The performance of simple approaches to spin-waiting

front: What code does Anderson's Table I give for a spin-on-test-and-set lock?
back: Init lock := CLEAR; Lock: while (TestAndSet(lock) = BUSY); Unlock: lock := CLEAR

front: What are Anderson's two named causes of spin-on-test-and-set degradation?
back: (1) To release, the holder must contend with spinners for exclusive access to the lock location, and most architectures cannot give the holder's clear request priority, so release waits behind doomed test-and-sets; (2) spinners' requests slow all other memory traffic, causing a hot-spot on multistage networks and bus saturation (each test-and-set is at least one bus transaction regardless of whether it changes the value).

text:
Anderson's spin-on-read release cascade:
  1. On release, {{c1::all cache copies are invalidated}}
  2. Each spinner {{c2::read-misses to refetch the lock; the misses are satisfied serially}}
  3. Each processor that gets the value {{c3::tries a test-and-set; the first succeeds, and any that finished its read miss before that saw the lock free, does a doomed test-and-set, fails, and resumes spinning}}
  4. Each failing test-and-set, being a write, {{c4::re-invalidates all copies, forcing those processors to miss again}}
The system quiesces only when {{c5::the last spinner finally test-and-sets}}.

front: On a fixed-priority machine like the Firefly, how can spin-on-read fail to protect the high-priority holder?
back: If the lock is released before quiescence, a low-priority processor with a pending test-and-set can grab it ahead of higher-priority processors still looping on read, and the holder can then be delayed by those higher-priority processors.

front: How does distributed-write help spin-on-read, and which machines use a separate distributed-write bus for test-and-set variables?
back: It eliminates invalidations (each processor receives updates directly, all reads are local, only test-and-sets need the bus); the Sequent Balance and Silicon Graphics 4D-MP each use a separate distributed-write bus just for test-and-set variables.
source: III.C: Reasons for the poor performance of spin on read

front: What is Anderson's measurement platform in Section III.D?
back: A Sequent Symmetry Model B with twenty 80386 processors (about 2 MIP each), shared bus, write-back invalidation-based coherence; unlike the Balance, test-and-set variables share the normal memory bus.

front: How long does acquiring and releasing a lock normally take on Anderson's Symmetry?
back: 5.6 microseconds (less if the lock's cache block is already private to the locker).

front: How is Anderson's benchmark (Fig. 1) constructed?
back: Each processor loops one million / P times doing acquire, critical section, release, and a random delay from a uniform distribution with mean five times the critical-section size; the random wait deliberately eliminates locality so lock and shared data move between caches each iteration, and lock and shared data are in separate cache blocks.

front: How does Anderson define the "ideal" curve?
back: The time the test would take given free spin-waiting, determined by simulation from the critical-section time and the mean inter-access delay.

front: What does Anderson's Fig. 1 plot and show?
back: Actual elapsed time (not just overhead) for spin-on-test-and-set, spin-on-read, and ideal: spin-on-test-and-set degrades badly; spin-on-read is better but still disappointing; peak ideal performance is never reached; performance is very sensitive to adding even a few processors past saturation.

front: What degenerative-feedback observation does Anderson make about critical sections?
back: Critical sections have higher memory-access rates than non-critical code (their purpose is to touch shared structures), so as a lock becomes a bottleneck the spinners slow the holder both absolutely and relatively, making it more of a bottleneck and spawning yet more spinners.

front: What is Anderson's Fig. 2 / quiesce experiment, and what does it find?
back: He measures time-to-quiesce with a critical section that first delays without using the bus and then uses it heavily; varying the initial delay finds a sharp "knee". The time to quiesce grows steeply but linearly with the number of spinning processors, so even a few spinners hurt a moderate critical section.

front: What five software approaches does Anderson's Section IV describe?
back: Four delay-based approaches (from CSMA network protocols) plus explicit queueing.

front: Along what two dimensions does Anderson organize the four delay variants?
back: Where the delay goes (after the lock is released, Table III; or after every reference, Table IV) crossed with how the delay is set (static or dynamic). Lock latency is unaffected because a processor tries to acquire the lock before delaying.

front: What CSMA lineage does Anderson give for the delay variants?
back: Statically assigned slots resemble BRAM (Chlamtac et al.); static delays resemble Aloha; dynamic backoff is Ethernet's exponential backoff (Metcalfe and Boggs). Slots can also implement priority access by assigning lower delays to higher-priority processors.

front: How do static slots work in Anderson's scheme, and what do they guarantee?
back: Each processor gets a slot 0..P-1; the smallest-delay spinner reacquires, the rest time out, see the lock busy (another cache miss), and resume. Static slots guarantee at most one processor times out at an instant.

front: How does the number of static slots trade off the two contention regimes?
back: Fewer slots is better with few spinners (faster handoff); more slots is better with many spinners (fewer simultaneous timeouts).

front: How does exponential backoff estimate spinner count, and what rule follows?
back: A processor estimates the number of spinners from the number of collisions; a collision is unlikely once the mean delay is at least half the number of spinners, so Ethernet doubles the mean delay after each collision. For locks, a processor doubles its mean delay each time it times out, sees the lock free, test-and-sets, and fails.

text:
Three backoff design details Anderson's first implementation got wrong:
  1. {{c1::Do not change the mean delay merely because another processor had a shorter delay}} (seeing the lock acquired says little about the number of spinners)
  2. {{c2::Bound the mean delay, with the bound equal to the number of processors}}, so backoff matches static slots under heavy contention
  3. {{c3::Start each visit at a fraction (he used half) of the previous delay rather than from zero}}, because the learning curve is expensive for locks

front: How do backoff and static slots behave under non-random (fixed-interval) and bursty arrivals, per Anderson?
back: With fixed-interval arrivals, processors self-schedule into either no contention or a steady number of spinners; backoff raises delays until collisions are rare and hysteresis maintains them. Both degrade on repeated bursty arrivals (all choose small delays, collide, take long to quiesce) and both end a burst with inappropriately long delays.

front: What applicability limit does Anderson give for polling-for-release, including the remote-directory cap?
back: It is only practical with per-processor coherent caches; otherwise spinners consume bandwidth. Some remote-directory multistage machines cap the number of outstanding copies of a location, so if spinners exceed the cap, spin-on-read degenerates to spinning across the network.

front: Even with snoopy or full-directory invalidation, what problem do backoff and static slots NOT fix?
back: They fix only one of the spin-on-read problems: each spinner still needs at least two read misses per critical section (one on release, one on acquire), which can saturate the bus.

front: On which machines is backoff-after-release specifically scalable, per Anderson?
back: On distributed-write machines, where each test-and-set is one broadcast bus cycle independent of P and backoff limits the number of failing test-and-sets.

front: Why does delay-between-each-reference check the lock before the test-and-set, and when does backoff behave badly for it?
back: It checks the lock first because a test-and-set costs more bandwidth than a read. Backoff here behaves badly for a single spinner on a moderate critical section: the processor keeps backing off while the lock is held and is then mid-delay when the lock is released, so it is slow to notice.

front: Why does a shared counter of spinners fail as an approach to queueing, per Anderson?
back: It costs two extra atomics per critical section and, worse, every spinner must read it to compute its delay, which on non-distributed-write systems consumes as much bandwidth as polling the lock directly.

front: Why does a naive explicit queue fail as an approach, per Anderson?
back: It requires locking the enqueue/dequeue operations, which must modify more than one location (even the VAX atomic enqueue/dequeue are slow), giving much worse performance for small critical sections.

front: What is the per-architecture best implementation of Anderson's queueing lock?
back: With distributed-write, all processors spin on a single counter and the releaser just writes its sequence number (one bus transaction updates the next); with invalidation, each flag goes in a separate cache block (two transactions, an invalidation and a read miss, to signal the next); on a multistage network without caches, each flag goes in a separate memory module.

front: Why is Anderson's queueing lock less valuable on a bus without coherence?
back: Processors must still poll, swamping the bus; a delay between polls (depending on queue distance and critical-section length) helps, and this is one way to use fewer than P locations, by polling rarely until close to the front.

front: What does Anderson say about the Symmetry's atomic support for his queueing lock?
back: If there is no atomic read-and-increment, the operation can itself be locked; it is only a few instructions so it rarely bottlenecks except with trivial critical sections or bursty arrivals, where a delay alternative should guard it. The Symmetry supports an atomic increment but not an atomic read-and-increment (the original value is not saved), so his measured queueing lock uses a backoff-protected sequence number.

front: What is the preemption downside of Anderson's queueing lock, and one mitigation?
back: Normally if the lock holder is preempted all its spinners wait, but with queueing, preempting any spin-waiting process forces everyone behind it to wait if it reaches the front before being rescheduled, causing lock-step behaviour for small, frequently accessed critical sections (cites Zahorjan et al.). Mitigation: if a process can be warned before preemption, it removes itself from the queue by tapping the next process.

front: What delay range and test-and-set cost does Anderson report for the software-alternatives measurements?
back: Static and dynamic delays ranged 0 to 15 microseconds; a test-and-set takes about one microsecond on the Symmetry.

front: What does Anderson's Fig. 3 plot, and what does the one-processor point represent?
back: Spin-waiting overhead (elapsed minus the ideal curve), not raw time; it includes spin-on-read for comparison but not spin-on-test-and-set. All five new methods have reasonable performance across the range. The one-processor point is lock latency: queueing has high latency, all others low (queueing would have lower latency with a hardware read-and-increment).

front: What does Anderson's Fig. 4 (overhead vs number of static slots) show?
back: Few slots win with few spinners, many slots win with many; the tradeoff sharpens as the maximum spinner count grows (64 slots has much worse low-load performance than plain spin-on-read, yet may be needed to avoid bad high-load performance). Backoff avoids the tradeoff by doing well in both regimes.

front: What is Anderson's Fig. 5 burst-arrival experiment, and what does it find?
back: Processors are released from a barrier and each then acquires the lock and bumps a counter, with overhead normalized per processor. Queueing does not do well at high processor counts because its sequence-number lock uses backoff; with two processors arriving together, static mean delay is worst; and all methods are bad because of initial contention.

front: What general tradeoff does Anderson note before describing hardware solutions?
back: The best coherence mechanism for spin locks may differ from the best for normal references; separate-bus solutions (Balance, 4D-MP) add expense of little benefit to applications that do not spin much, and can even hurt latency if the spin-lock bus is slower.

front: How do combining networks help spin locks, and what is the caveat?
back: They merge requests to the same location at a switch (cites Pfister and Norton): two test-and-sets combine so only one is forwarded, and a test-and-set combined with a clear forwards the set while the test-and-set returns having acquired the lock. Combining gives good performance for any number of spinners, but combining switches are more complex and likely slower, so a normal network with backoff or queueing might beat it.

front: How does hardware queueing at the memory module work, per Anderson?
back: Processors issue explicit "enter" and "exit" critical-section instructions and the module maintains per-lock queues, so when an "enter" returns the processor holds the lock with no polling. This eliminates one network round trip relative to software queueing and likely gives better latency despite added module complexity.

front: What did Goodman et al. propose for hardware queueing?
back: Holding queue links in the caches themselves (the next processor's name stored in each cache), so release notifies the next processor without going through the memory module, and optionally returning control to software after enqueueing so the processor is separately notified when it reaches the front.

front: Why does the naive snoopy fix (invalidate only if the lock value actually changes) solve only one problem?
back: On release there is still an invalidation, a cache miss per spinner, and some failing test-and-sets, so time-to-quiesce shrinks but does not vanish and performance still degrades as spinners grow, unlike backoff or queueing.

front: What is read-broadcast, and whom does Anderson cite for it?
back: A cache controller watching the bus that sees a read for a block it holds invalid takes the data off the bus and validates its own copy, so one read fills all caches and the cascade of read misses is eliminated without full distributed-write; a controller with a pending read that sees another processor granted a read to the same location should just take that returning data. Cites Segall and Rudolph, and Karlin et al.

front: In Anderson's special test-and-set handling, what does the cache/bus controller do on a test-and-set that would fail?
back: It does not commit a test-and-set to the bus while it might fail: it checks the cache (read-missing, possibly served by read-broadcast, if absent), and if the lock is busy it returns immediately without using the bus.

front: In Anderson's special test-and-set handling, what does the controller do once it sees the lock free?
back: Only then does it arbitrate for the bus, meanwhile monitoring the bus: it aborts the pending test-and-set if the value is broadcast busy (distributed-write), or converts it back to a read if the block is invalidated.

front: Why does special test-and-set handling need extra information, and how is correctness preserved?
back: Cache controllers do not normally know an atomic's type (the ALU does), so the cache needs extra information to abort pending test-and-sets. Correctness is preserved because the processor's actions are consistent with some serial ordering of atomics.

front: Under what condition does Anderson say special test-and-set handling beats software backoff or queueing, and why?
back: If it does not raise the cycle time; software backoff and queueing never reach ideal performance on the Symmetry (Fig. 3).

front: What are Anderson's hardware findings in the conclusion, and what question is left open?
back: On multistage networks, explicit hardware queueing (at the module or in caches) cuts the handoff time; on shared buses, failing test-and-sets can be handled with no bus traffic given more intelligent snooping. Whether real workloads spin enough to justify such hardware is left as an open question.
